paragraphs: I studied abroad at Tulane University for three months. It was difficult to take part while the supervising doctors and residents discussed specialized content in English, but I took part actively, recalling how to cut into a discussion that I had been taught in the pre-departure training. Here I describe what I did and felt in this clinical clerkship abroad.

One of the things that left the strongest impression during my study abroad was being able to attend the American College of Physicians Internal Medicine Meeting (American College of Physicians conference) held in New Orleans. Doctors gathered in a vast venue not only from all over the United States but from countries around the world, and the usually busy town was even more festive, like a kind of dream. I was able to talk with famous internists and listen to presentations, and I feel very honored to have been able to go while still a student. The young doctors who came from Japan were also very stimulating. Seeing a doctor who, in their first year of residency, won a conference presentation with their own research, and doctors who, as Japan's representatives in Doctor's Dilemma, competed with native speakers in medical knowledge, I reaffirmed that residency can be anything depending on motivation and effort, and I felt myself tighten up.
I did clerkships in a total of four departments, and among them were some that do not exist in clerkships in Japan, which was very interesting.

(A) Hospice. In the two-week clerkship at the hospice, every day I rode in a car with a nurse or volunteer to do home-visit nursing, performing physical examination, pressure ulcer care and medication management. In addition, in the United States there is a role called Chaplain, who cares for patients from a religious aspect, and I once accompanied one to a funeral. Sometimes a patient I was following died, and it was hard because, the week before, I had said goodbye saying, "I will come again, so let's be sure to meet next week."

(B) Culinary Medicine. If rendered in Japanese it would be 料理医学. It is a cooking class opened by a person who changed from chef to doctor, lamenting that doctors and medical students know far too little about nutrition, and it teaches doctors, medical students, patients and the general public how to make meals that are good for health. For example, I taught patients with heart failure how to make meals with salt kept below 2.4 g/day. In addition, a representative of a major convenience store chain was invited and proposed convenience store meals with reduced salt and fat. At the end of the clerkship I was also given the opportunity to give a presentation on unsaturated fatty acids based on a new paper, and I was satisfied that I was able to show the results of my clerkship.

(C) Orthopedic surgery. The orthopedic surgery clerkship was mainly observing operations. Tulane University functions as a very large trauma center, and I was allowed into the surgical field for amputation operations. American residents on the whole are older than Japanese residents, but seeing a female resident pulling the patient's leg throughout the operation to secure the view of the hip joint, I was overwhelmed by her stamina and strength. However, discharge is truly early, such as discharging patients the day after total knee arthroplasty, and there were points at which I thought patients might feel great anxiety.

(D) Pathology. Tulane's pathology is divided into Surgical pathology and Clinical pathology, and I did my clerkship in Surgical pathology and received explanations of specimens. There were also definitions that differ, such as carcinoma in situ in Japan not being classified as cancer in the United States, which was interesting. In addition, Tulane University uses a chart dictation system, in which doctors record what they want to write in the chart and several chart-writing staff in the hospital type it, so there was the advantage that pathologists, even when both hands are occupied while cutting out specimens, can record with a pedal at their feet and make chart entries. However, once a recording could not be matched to which patient it belonged to, and the chart was not written the next morning, and I could also see the disadvantage of the person stating the findings being different from the person actually writing the chart.

Before going to the United States I had the impression that the United States is the advanced country in medicine and a vague preconception that the medicine practiced there must be the best. However, after actually doing a clerkship for three months, my impression was that Japan provides medical care that is better for patients. In the United States there are conferences called grand rounds, where one can hear presentations of clinical research done within the hospital or lectures by doctors invited from other hospitals, and I thought it was educational. But it is hard to evaluate whether what is newly obtained in research is reflected in clinical practice, and I thought that in the quality of medical care seen from the patient's side, such as cooperation between hospitals and postoperative care, Japan is superior. Therefore, I now want to work in Japan in the future.
I would like to thank everyone, beginning with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, who arranged and supported this study abroad.
